OCI container images follow the OCI Image Format Specification, which defines how image manifests, metadata, configuration, and filesystem layers are structured and exchanged. Because they follow an open standard, OCI images can be created, stored, and consumed by different container tools such as Docker, Podman, etc.

On a host machine, an OCI image is not stored as one ordinary project file. It is persisted through the container manager's internal storage logic, which manages image metadata, shared filesystem layers, and writable container layers. To inspect or move that content as a file, use a dedicated export format such as the OCI image-layout TAR archive, Docker image TAR archive or as a flat filesystem archive from a container (docker export).

docs.title: Pros
docs.text:
• ✅ Bundles the application and runtime
  • ✅ Isolates dependencies from the host
  • ✅ Runs consistently across container platforms
  • ✅ Supports reliable rollbacks

docs.title: Cons
docs.text:
• ⚠️ Requires container infrastructure
  • ⚠️ Images can be large
  • ⚠️ Base images require regular patching
  • ⚠️ Data and secrets need separate management

docs.title: Packaging Workflow
docs.text:
Info

This workflow assumes that you have a valid Cloudsmith repository and access to its Docker registry. Set CLOUDSMITH_REPOSITORY to the Cloudsmith owner and repository path, such as example-org/python-containers, before you publish.

docs.title: Create the Environment
docs.text:
License Service uses a runtime Dockerfile, not a Dev Container. The image build installs uv and the application dependencies as part of the image creation, so the host only needs Docker and the project source tree.

First, confirm that Docker is installed and running on the host machine:

docker version

Move into the License Service project directory:

cd projects/proj2_license_service

Set the Cloudsmith repository that will receive the published image:

export CLOUDSMITH_REPOSITORY="<owner>/<repository>"

docs.title: Create the Package
docs.text:
The same Dockerfile can produce different output formats depending on the build command. The first workflow creates a normal local image managed by Docker, while the second creates a portable OCI image archive as a file on disk.

Classical container imageOCI image archive

This command builds the image from the Dockerfile, stores the resulting image layers and metadata in Docker's local image store, and assigns the tag license-service:1.0.0. The image can then be inspected, run, tagged for a registry, or pushed from the local Docker host.

docker build -t license-service:1.0.0 .

List local container images to confirm that the build produced the tagged image:

docker image ls

This command uses BuildKit through docker buildx to build the image and write it directly to image.tar as an OCI image layout archive. The archive contains OCI metadata and content-addressed blobs, but it is not loaded into Docker's local image store unless you import it later.

docker buildx build \
  --output type=oci,dest=license-service-1.0.0.tar \
  .

docs.title: Inspect the Package
docs.text:
The inspection command depends on the output format created in the previous step. A local Docker image is inspected through the container manager's image store, while an OCI image archive is inspected as files inside the TAR archive.

Classical container imageOCI image archive

Inspect the metadata that Docker stores for the local image tag:

docker inspect license-service:1.0.0

The output includes the image ID, content digests, environment variables, entry point, exposed ports, platform, and layer metadata that Docker uses to create containers from the image.

Show the image layer history and the Dockerfile instruction associated with each layer:

docker history license-service:1.0.0

Inspect the archive created by docker buildx build --output type=oci by listing the files inside the TAR archive:

tar -tf license-service-1.0.0.tar

The exported OCI archive has a structure similar to this:

license-service-1.0.0.tar
├── blobs/
│   └── sha256/
│       ├── <digest> (manifest JSON)
│       ├── <digest> (configuration JSON)
│       ├── <digest> (filesystem layer)
│       └── ...
├── index.json
└── oci-layout
  • oci-layout: Identifies the archive as an OCI image layout and records the layout version.
  • index.json: Acts as the archive entry point. It points to the image manifest stored under blobs/sha256/ and can associate that manifest with a tag.
  • blobs/sha256/<digest>: Stores all content-addressed image objects. Some blobs are JSON documents, such as the image manifest and image configuration, while other blobs are compressed filesystem layers.

docs.title: Publish the Package
docs.text:
Published images are addressed by a repository and tag, such as python:3.12-slim, while registries resolve that tag to an immutable digest such as sha256:<digest>. Tags are readable and convenient, but they can be reassigned; pulling by digest, for example docker pull python@sha256:<digest>, guarantees the same image content across environments.

To publish the image, set CLOUDSMITH_REPOSITORY to the Cloudsmith owner and repository path, such as example-org/python-containers. Do not include the registry host or image name in this value.

export CLOUDSMITH_REPOSITORY="<owner>/<repository>"

Then authenticate with Cloudsmith's Docker registry:

docker login docker.cloudsmith.io

Tag the local image with the Cloudsmith registry path:

docker tag license-service:1.0.0 "docker.cloudsmith.io/${CLOUDSMITH_REPOSITORY}/license-service:1.0.0"

Then upload the tagged image:

docker push "docker.cloudsmith.io/${CLOUDSMITH_REPOSITORY}/license-service:1.0.0"

docs.title: Install the Container
docs.text:
Once published, the image can be downloaded from Cloudsmith:

docker pull "docker.cloudsmith.io/${CLOUDSMITH_REPOSITORY}/license-service:1.0.0"

To run the packaged service, you can leverage the run command:

docker run -p 8080:8080 "docker.cloudsmith.io/${CLOUDSMITH_REPOSITORY}/license-service:1.0.0"

Confirm that the service responds:

curl http://127.0.0.1:8080/

docs.title: Conda Packages
docs.text:
Conda packages distribute Python projects together with managed dependencies from the Conda ecosystem. Unlike Python wheels, which primarily distribute Python packages, Conda packages can bundle Python modules, native libraries, command-line tools, and software from multiple language ecosystems.

The Conda workflow connects project definition, multi-language dependency resolution, package building, package hosting, and local installation. A recipe declares Python modules and native libraries; the built .conda artifacts carry that dependency graph; a channel exposes package metadata through platform-specific indexes; and a local environment installs the Python and native components into one prefix.

docs.title: Project Setup
docs.text:
The applied project is IrisLab, a small image-based iris color analysis application. It uses MediaPipe Face Landmarker with a local machine-learning model to locate the irises in real photos, then analyzes the extracted pixels with NumPy and CIELAB color space to determine perceptual color features and classify the eye color. The resulting color profile is compared with reference colors using a native C++ library that calculates CIE ΔE color distances and is exposed to Python through pybind11. This makes IrisLab a good fit for Conda because a single environment manages Python packages, native libraries, compiled C++ code, and local machine-learning dependencies together.

The recipe produces two Conda packages:

Conda package Contents libirislab Standalone C++ shared library (libirislab.so, .dylib, or .dll) and the public irislab.hpp header. irislab-tools Python package, irislab CLI, and pybind11 extension. It depends on the matching libirislab build.

docs.title: Run the Project
docs.text: Application, test, lint, package-build, and shell-exit commands are documented in the project README.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
Conda packages are built distributions for multi-language software. Modern Conda packages use the .conda format, while older releases may use .tar.bz2; both contain a pre-built payload and package metadata so installation does not require compiling software on the target machine. Conda is commonly used for data science, scientific computing, native extensions, and environments that combine Python with C, C++, R, CUDA, or other runtimes.

Conda distribution has four primary building blocks. A package format stores the payload and generated metadata, a recipe describes how the package is built and which dependencies it requires, a package manager resolves dependencies and creates isolated environments, and a channel stores packages with searchable indexes. Build tools such as conda-build transform a recipe into platform-specific Conda packages before they are published to a channel.

Building Block Role Common Examples Package Format Stores the built payload together with generated package metadata. .conda, .tar.bz2 Build Recipe Defines package metadata, build instructions, dependencies, and tests. recipe/meta.yaml, recipe/recipe.yaml Package Manager Resolves dependencies and creates or updates isolated environments. conda, mamba, micromamba, pixi Remote Repository Publishes packages and channel indexes for supported platforms and architectures. conda-forge, Anaconda.org, Cloudsmith

docs.title: Project Layout
docs.text:
A Conda package is built with a dedicated recipe directory alongside the project source code.

{project_root}/
├── cpp/
│   ├── CMakeLists.txt
│   ├── bindings.cpp
│   ├── irislab.cpp
│   └── irislab.hpp
├── recipe/
│   ├── build-irislab-tools.bat
│   ├── build-irislab-tools.sh
│   ├── build-libirislab.bat
│   ├── build-libirislab.sh
│   └── meta.yaml
├── samples/
├── src/
│   └── irislab/
├── tests/
├── environment.yml
└── README.md
  • recipe/meta.yaml: Defines the two Conda outputs, their dependencies, build steps, entry point, and package tests.
  • cpp/: Contains the native C++ scoring library, public header, pybind11 bindings, and CMake configuration.
  • src/: Contains the Python package and CLI.
  • environment.yml: Defines the development environment, including runtime, native, and testing dependencies, plus the pip-only mediapipe package.

docs.title: Package Recipe
docs.text:
A Conda package is defined by a YAML recipe that declares package identity, source, build behavior, dependencies, tests, and descriptive metadata. IrisLab uses a multi-output recipe so the standalone native library and Python package remain separately reusable.

outputs:
  # -------------------------------------------------------------------------
  # libirislab: standalone C++ shared library and headers.
  # -------------------------------------------------------------------------
  - name: libirislab
    script: build-libirislab.sh

    build:
      run_exports:
        - {{ pin_subpackage('libirislab', max_pin='x.x') }}

    requirements:
      build:
        - "{{ compiler('cxx') }}"
        - cmake
        - ninja

  # -------------------------------------------------------------------------
  # irislab-tools: Python package, CLI, and pybind11 extension.
  #
  # The extension is built directly with CMake and links against libirislab.
  # -------------------------------------------------------------------------
  - name: irislab-tools

    script: build-irislab-tools.sh   # [unix]
    script: build-irislab-tools.bat  # [win]

    build:
      entry_points:
        - irislab = irislab.cli:main

    requirements:
      build:
        - "{{ compiler('cxx') }}"
        - cmake
        - ninja

      host:
        - python >=3.12
        - pybind11 >=2.12
        - {{ pin_subpackage('libirislab', exact=True) }}

      run:
        - python >=3.12
        - click
        - pillow
        - rich
        - numpy
        - glib
        - libgl
        - libegl
        - libgles
        - {{ pin_subpackage('libirislab', exact=True) }}

    test:
      requires:
        - pip

      imports:
        - irislab
        - irislab._native

      commands:
        - python -m pip install mediapipe
        - irislab --help
  • libirislab: Builds the standalone C++ shared library and public header. Its run_exports entry provides a compatible library pin to downstream packages.
  • irislab-tools: Builds the Python package and pybind11 extension. Its exact pin_subpackage dependency ensures the extension uses the matching native library.
  • requirements.host: Supplies Python and native build dependencies while the package is compiled.
  • requirements.run: Records the dependencies needed by the installed application.
  • test: Installs the PyPI-only MediaPipe dependency, then verifies that the extension imports and the generated CLI is available.

docs.title: Package Layout
docs.text:
A .conda file is a ZIP container with separate compressed metadata and payload archives. IrisLab produces two packages from one recipe, allowing C/C++ consumers to install libirislab without the Python stack while Python consumers install irislab-tools and receive the native library automatically.

libirislab — C/C++ payloadirislab-tools — Python payload 
libirislab-1.0.0-<build>.conda
├── metadata.json
├── info-*.tar.zst
│   └── info/
│       ├── about.json
│       ├── index.json                 # depends: compiler runtimes and run_exports
│       └── recipe/meta.yaml
└── pkg-*.tar.zst
    ├── include/
    │   └── irislab.hpp
    └── lib/
        └── libirislab.so

irislab-tools-1.0.0-<build>.conda
├── metadata.json
├── info-*.tar.zst
│   └── info/index.json              # depends: libirislab, pillow, rich
└── pkg-*.tar.zst
    ├── bin/
    │   └── irislab
    └── site-packages/
        ├── irislab/
        │   ├── __init__.py
        │   ├── cli.py
        │   ├── eye_color.py
        │   ├── iris.py
        │   ├── analyze.py
        │   └── _native.<platform>.so

docs.title: Pros
docs.text:
• ✅ Manages Python and native dependencies
  • ✅ Supports compiled libraries
  • ✅ Creates isolated environments
  • ✅ Provides platform-specific channels

docs.title: Cons
docs.text:
• ⚠️ Dependency solving can be slow
  • ⚠️ Requires platform-specific builds
  • ⚠️ Mixing pip can reduce reproducibility
  • ⚠️ Channel priorities add complexity

docs.title: Packaging Workflow
docs.text:
Info

This workflow assumes that you have a valid Cloudsmith repository and API key. Replace <cloudsmith-repo> with your Cloudsmith repository slug, export CLOUDSMITH_API_KEY on the host, and pass both values into the container.

docs.title: Create the Environment
docs.text:
For the Conda environment and C++ extension build, see Python Conda Environments. Its Dockerfile.devEnv image installs Miniconda, configures conda-forge, and includes the compiler toolchain, MediaPipe model, and project files. Choose the workflow that matches the local mpe/proj3_irislab image:

Image does not existImage already exists

From the projects/ directory, use build.sh to build and open the interactive packaging container. The command enables GPU access and forwards the Cloudsmith configuration:

./build.sh build \
  --path proj3_irislab/Dockerfile.devEnv \
  --gpus all \
  --cloudsmith-workspace "<cloudsmith-repo>" \
  --cloudsmith-api-key "$CLOUDSMITH_API_KEY"

From the projects/ directory, create the host directory for package artifacts and run the existing image:

mkdir -p proj3_irislab/.build
docker run -it \
  -v "$PWD/proj3_irislab:/app" \
  -v "$PWD/proj3_irislab/.build:/opt/conda/conda-bld" \
  -e CLOUDSMITH_REPOSITORY="<cloudsmith-repo>" \
  -e CLOUDSMITH_API_KEY="$CLOUDSMITH_API_KEY" \
  mpe/proj3_irislab \
  /bin/bash

Install the packaging tools in Conda's base environment rather than in the project's irislab environment. This separation keeps the Packaging Workflow independent from the Development Workflow.

conda install \
    --name base \
    --channel conda-forge \
    conda-build \
    conda-package-handling
  • conda-build: Builds Conda packages from recipes.
  • conda-package-handling: Provides cph for listing package archives and inspecting their metadata and contents.

The following command runs pip in Conda's base environment. It downloads the cloudsmith-cli package from PyPI and installs it for uploading packages to the configured Cloudsmith repository.

conda run --name base python -m pip install cloudsmith-cli==1.26.0

docs.title: Create the Package
docs.text:
Activate the base environment before running the packaging command:

conda activate base

Clear previous (Conda) build artifacts from the default artifact output directory:

find "/opt/conda/conda-bld" -mindepth 1 -delete

From the project root, build both packages with conda build. The --channel conda-forge option provides the public compilers, CMake, Python, Pillow, and other dependencies required by the recipe.

conda build recipe/ --channel conda-forge

conda-build invokes the recipe scripts automatically. It first builds libirislab, then builds the _native Python extension against that package. You do not need to run CMake separately for the packaging workflow. conda-build writes packages to /opt/conda/conda-bld inside the container. The project .build directory is bind-mounted there, so the package artifacts remain available on the host.

  • libirislab: Provides the standalone native C++ library and public header.
  • irislab-tools: Provides the Python package, CLI, and pybind11 extension.

docs.title: Inspect the Package
docs.text:
The two archives have different payloads and dependency metadata, so inspect them separately. The native package should declare compiler runtime dependencies such as libgcc and libstdcxx, together with a run_exports entry. The Python package should declare an exact dependency on the matching libirislab build.

libirislabirislab-tools

Resolve the native package created in the previous step:

LIBIRISLAB_PKG="$(find "/opt/conda/conda-bld" -type f -name 'libirislab-*.conda' -print -quit)"

List the package contents:

cph list "$LIBIRISLAB_PKG"

Extract and inspect its metadata:

cph extract --info --dest /tmp/libirislab-info "$LIBIRISLAB_PKG"
cat /tmp/libirislab-info/info/index.json

Resolve the Python package created in the previous step:

IRISLAB_TOOLS_PKG="$(find "/opt/conda/conda-bld" -type f -name 'irislab-tools-*.conda' -print -quit)"

List the package contents:

cph list "$IRISLAB_TOOLS_PKG"

Extract and inspect its metadata:

cph extract --info --dest /tmp/irislab-tools-info "$IRISLAB_TOOLS_PKG"
cat /tmp/irislab-tools-info/info/index.json

docs.title: Publish the Package
docs.text:
A compiled Conda package is built for a target platform. The channel organizes those artifacts under platform directories and exposes each directory through a generated repodata.json index. Because this recipe emits two outputs, each platform receives both a libirislab-*.conda and a irislab-tools-*.conda artifact.

repository-root/
├── linux-64/
│   ├── repodata.json
│   ├── libirislab-1.0.0-<build>.conda
│   └── irislab-tools-1.0.0-<build>.conda
├── osx-arm64/
│   ├── repodata.json
│   ├── libirislab-1.0.0-<build>.conda
│   └── irislab-tools-1.0.0-<build>.conda
└── win-64/
    ├── repodata.json
    ├── libirislab-1.0.0-<build>.conda
    └── irislab-tools-1.0.0-<build>.conda

Upload the two archives created in the previous step so the exact native-library pin can be satisfied at install time:

mapfile -t PACKAGES < <(find "/opt/conda/conda-bld" -type f \( \
  -name 'libirislab-*.conda' -o -name 'irislab-tools-*.conda' \
\) -print)
for PACKAGE in "${PACKAGES[@]}"; do
    cloudsmith push conda "${CLOUDSMITH_REPOSITORY}" "$PACKAGE"
done

Verify that Cloudsmith received both artifacts:

cloudsmith list packages "${CLOUDSMITH_REPOSITORY}" -q "libirislab OR irislab-tools"

Python Wheels

A wheel workflow can publish platform-specific files under one Python project name, but a Python index does not solve the native libirislab dependency as a separate environment package. Conda keeps the native library, Python extension, and their dependency metadata visible to the solver.

docs.title: Configure the Package Manager
docs.text:
Configure .condarc before creating the environment. Replace <cloudsmith-repo> with the repository slug. Conda creates .condarc automatically when the first command writes to it.

Expose the Cloudsmith channel URL to your local environment:

CLOUDSMITH_CHANNEL="https://token:${CLOUDSMITH_API_KEY}@conda.cloudsmith.io/<cloudsmith-repo>/"

Clear existing channels:

conda config --remove-key channels

Add the required channels:

conda config --add channels nodefaults
conda config --add channels conda-forge
conda config --add channels "$CLOUDSMITH_CHANNEL"

Set strict channel priority:

conda config --set channel_priority strict

docs.title: Install the Package
docs.text:
Create a small consumer project:

mkdir irislab-consumer && cd irislab-consumer

Record the irislab-tools package as an environment dependency:

name: irislab-demo
dependencies:
  - python=3.12
  - irislab-tools

Then, create the environment:

conda env create --file environment.yml

Both irislab-tools and its exact libirislab dependency get installed.

Activate the consumer environment:

conda activate irislab-demo

Since mediapipe is not available from conda-forge, install it from PyPI:

conda run --name "irislab-demo" python -m pip install mediapipe

The CLI accepts a portrait image and analyzes the detected iris color:

irislab --image samples/blue-eyes.png

The project also exposes a Python API:

from irislab import analyze

result = analyze("samples/blue-eye.png")

print(result.eye_color)
print(result.lab)
print(result.closest_profile)
print(result.delta_e)

docs.title: Introduction
docs.text: Chapter 03 introduces uv, Astral's Rust-based Python project and package manager, first released in 2024. Its project configuration centers on pyproject.toml, which records project metadata and dependencies, while its lockfile supports reproducible installs. The chapter covers scaffolding workspaces, managing and caching dependencies, building and publishing packages, and workflows for standalone scripts, environments, and command-line tools with uvx or uv pip.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
Use the navigation on the left to move through the chapter's sections:

Section Summary Project Notebook Section 01 Project scaffolding with uv - A New Hope for Bob Section 02 Dependency management with uv - Bob Discovers the Force of uv Section 03 Dependency caching with uv Bob Follows the Cache Section 03 Using uv's cache in CI uv-cache.yml - Section 04 Standalone environments and tools with uv - Modern Python with uv

docs.title: Introduction
docs.text: This section shows how to use uv to scaffold a multi-project workspace, initialize its backend and frontend components, and configure project metadata and shared workspace settings in pyproject.toml and uv.lock. The example pairs a Bottle backend with a Streamlit frontend.

docs.title: The Modern Python Standard
docs.text:
The pyproject.toml is the modern standard to describe a Python project. PEP 518 established it for build-system requirements, PEP 621 standardized project metadata, and PEP 735 standardized dependency groups. Together with tool-specific settings, these entries bring project metadata, build configuration, and dependency declarations that were often scattered across setup.py, setup.cfg, and requirements.txt into one clear source of truth. Exact resolved versions belong in the lockfile, which helps keep installations consistent and reduces environment drift.

uv builds its project workflows around pyproject.toml and the lockfile. It writes project metadata and dependency declarations to the project file and uses the lockfile to keep environments consistent. A small web backend could keep these settings together in one file:

[build-system]
requires = ["uv_build>=0.11.8,<0.12"]
build-backend = "uv_build"

[project]
name = "example-web-app"
version = "0.1.0"
requires-python = ">=3.12"
dependencies = [
    "bottle>=0.13",
]

[dependency-groups]
dev = [
    "pytest>=8.0",
    "ruff>=0.15",
]

[tool.ruff]
line-length = 88

docs.title: Install uv
docs.text:
uv is distributed as a single, self-contained static binary and can be installed without Python already present.

macOS and LinuxWindows

Run the standalone installer in a terminal:

curl -LsSf https://astral.sh/uv/install.sh | sh

Run the standalone installer in PowerShell:

powershell -ExecutionPolicy ByPass -c "irm https://astral.sh/uv/install.ps1 | iex"

Check that the command is available:

uv --version

docs.title: Manage Python with uv
docs.text:
Like nvm for Node.js and rustup for Rust, uv can install and select interpreter versions without replacing the system interpreter. Use the uv python commands to manage interpreters. Install version 3.12 alongside the system interpreter:

uv python install 3.12

On Linux, uv stores managed interpreter files in ~/.local/share/uv/python by default. Run uv python dir to see the configured installation directory. The home-directory path varies by user:

uv python dir

docs.title: Create the Workspace
docs.text:
A uv workspace groups related projects under one root. Each component keeps its own pyproject.toml, while the workspace shares one uv.lock and resolves dependencies together. Here the workspace contains an HTTP backend and a browser-facing frontend; neither component depends on the other yet.

Initialize the workspace root as a bare project using Python 3.12. The root project owns the workspace configuration and the shared lockfile:

uv init --bare --python 3.12 --vcs none uv-workspace

Create directories for the two workspace members:

mkdir -p uv-workspace/backend uv-workspace/frontend

After both components are initialized, the root pyproject.toml lists them as workspace members. Each member owns its project metadata, dependencies, and local interpreter pin. The first dependency resolution creates the single root uv.lock.

docs.title: Pin Python for the Components
docs.text:
Both workspace members use Python 3.12. A .python-version file selects the interpreter for local commands; requires-python in each pyproject.toml declares the versions supported by that project. Workspace members must have compatible requires-python requirements, and using the same pin here makes that relationship explicit.

BackendFrontend

--no-project writes the pin before the member's pyproject.toml exists:

uv --directory uv-workspace/backend python pin --no-project 3.12

Use the same Python version for the frontend member:

uv --directory uv-workspace/frontend python pin --no-project 3.12

docs.title: Initialize the Workspace Components
docs.text:
Initialize each member as a packaged application. The template creates project metadata and starter package files; this section uses that generated scaffolding without implementing application modules.

BackendFrontend

The backend is a Python application that will provide HTTP endpoints. Initialize it as a packaged application, disabling Git initialization because the workspace root is the repository:

uv init --app --package --vcs none --author-from none uv-workspace/backend

When run inside an existing project, uv init discovers the workspace and registers the new project as a member. Inspect the member configuration:

cat uv-workspace/backend/pyproject.toml

The frontend will provide a small interactive UI with Streamlit. Initialize it as a separate packaged application in the same workspace:

uv init --app --package --vcs none --author-from none uv-workspace/frontend

Inspect the generated project metadata:

cat uv-workspace/frontend/pyproject.toml

Confirm that the root includes both projects as workspace members and that the lockfile is at the root:

cat uv-workspace/pyproject.toml

Each member has its own project metadata and Python pin, while the workspace has one lockfile at its root rather than one per component.

docs.title: Add a Workspace Dependency
docs.text:
The backend and frontend already share a workspace. Add a small library under packages/ to see how another project joins it. Create the parent directory:

mkdir -p uv-workspace/packages

Initialize a library. Because it is created inside the workspace, uv init adds it to the root workspace members:

uv init --lib --vcs none --author-from none uv-workspace/packages/shared-components

Inspect the root workspace configuration:

cat uv-workspace/pyproject.toml

Make the backend depend on the local library. --workspace records the dependency as a workspace source instead of fetching a package from an index:

uv --directory uv-workspace/backend add --workspace shared-components

Inspect the backend's dependency and workspace source:

cat uv-workspace/backend/pyproject.toml

This adds the library as a third workspace member and resolves all members into the single root lockfile. Workspace dependencies are installed editably during development.

docs.title: Add Dependencies and Run the Project
docs.text:
By default, uv add updates project metadata and the workspace lockfile, creates a virtual environment if needed, and installs dependencies. Run the commands from each member while addressing it explicitly with --directory.

BackendFrontend

Add Bottle, a small web framework, to the backend with an exact version requirement:

uv --directory uv-workspace/backend add "bottle==0.13.4"

Add Streamlit to the frontend: 

uv --directory uv-workspace/frontend add streamlit

The dependencies are recorded in each member's pyproject.toml, while uv.lock remains at the workspace root. The generated workspace tree now looks like this:

uv-workspace/
├── pyproject.toml
├── uv.lock
├── backend/
│   ├── .python-version
│   ├── README.md
│   ├── pyproject.toml
│   └── src/
│       └── backend/
│           └── __init__.py
└── frontend/
    ├── .python-version
    ├── README.md
    ├── pyproject.toml
    └── src/
        └── frontend/
            └── __init__.py

Inspect the backend metadata:

cat uv-workspace/backend/pyproject.toml

Inspect the frontend metadata:

cat uv-workspace/frontend/pyproject.toml

Inspect the root lockfile location:

ls uv-workspace/uv.lock

The generated package files are scaffolding only. No Bottle routes or Streamlit UI are implemented in this section. Once application code is added, uv run --directory uv-workspace/backend ... and uv run --directory uv-workspace/frontend ... run commands in the corresponding workspace project.

Add Ruff for linting and pytest for testing to the backend's dev dependency group, rather than its runtime requirements:

uv --directory uv-workspace/backend add --dev ruff pytest

Your Ruff and pytest versions may differ. uv writes compatible version ranges to project metadata and resolves exact versions in the shared uv.lock.

docs.title: Use the [tool.*] Table
docs.text:
Tools that support pyproject.toml can keep their settings alongside project metadata instead of using separate tool-specific configuration files. These tables configure tools but do not install them. Add Ruff and pytest settings to the backend project:

uv-workspace/backend/pyproject.toml
[tool.ruff]
line-length = 88

[tool.pytest.ini_options]
testpaths = ["tests"]
addopts = "-ra"

The workspace project files now hold component-specific metadata and settings, while dependency resolution is shared at the root. Put future backend tests in tests/; configuration alone does not create test files.

docs.title: Build a Package
docs.text:
Python packaging separates building into a frontend and a backend, with their interface defined by PEP 517. The build frontend coordinates the build, while the build backend creates installable distributions. PEP 518 defines how a project declares its build backend and requirements in [build-system].

The frontend in that packaging terminology is distinct from the Streamlit UI component. Common build frontends include python -m build, pip wheel, and uv build; common build backends include setuptools.build_meta, hatchling.build, and uv_build. The packaged application templates use uv_build in their [build-system] table.

Build the backend distributions from its project directory:

uv build uv-workspace/backend --out-dir uv-workspace/backend/dist

Build the frontend distributions:

uv build uv-workspace/frontend --out-dir uv-workspace/frontend/dist

The output directory is selected explicitly so each component's distributions remain with that component. Inspect the backend output:

ls -lah uv-workspace/backend/dist/

docs.title: Publish a Package
docs.text:
Before uploading, check the project name, version, and package contents. Set a PyPI token in UV_PUBLISH_TOKEN, then pass a component's distribution files to uv publish:

uv publish uv-workspace/backend/dist/*.whl uv-workspace/backend/dist/*.tar.gz

For a first trial, use TestPyPI with a TestPyPI token and its upload URL:

uv publish --publish-url https://test.pypi.org/legacy/ uv-workspace/backend/dist/*.whl uv-workspace/backend/dist/*.tar.gz

Repeat the publish command with uv-workspace/frontend/dist/*.whl and uv-workspace/frontend/dist/*.tar.gz when that component is ready to release. For more detail on wheel packaging and uploading distributions, see Chapter 02, Section 01.

docs.title: Introduction
docs.text: This section explains how uv manages project dependencies, from adding packages from indexes or Git repositories to organizing development tools and locking resolved versions for consistent environments. See adding dependencies, dependency groups, Git package sources, and the lockfile for details.

docs.title: Declaring Dependencies
docs.text:
uv provides dedicated commands for adding and removing dependencies. By default, these commands update the project's dependency declarations, resolve versions into a lockfile, and synchronize the virtual environment. Runtime requirements belong in the standard project dependency field, while other tables can describe development groups or tool-specific package sources.

Start with a project file that contains metadata but no dependencies:

[project]
name = "license-service"
version = "0.1.0"
requires-python = ">=3.11"

docs.title: Add from a Package Index
docs.text:
Use uv add to update the dependencies entry in pyproject.toml and immediately re-resolve. By default, uv selects the newest version compatible with the project's Python requirement and records it as a lower bound (>=):

uv add requests

To require an exact version, use the == constraint:

uv add "httpx==0.27.2"

To allow patch releases within the 0.115 series, specify a version range:

uv add "fastapi>=0.115,<0.116"

After these commands, the complete project file looks like this. NOTE that the requests lower bound may vary:

[project]
name = "license-service"
version = "0.1.0"
requires-python = ">=3.11"
dependencies = [
    "fastapi>=0.115,<0.116", # Allow patch releases in 0.115
    "httpx==0.27.2", # Require this exact version
    "requests>=2.32.3", # Set a minimum version
]

Choosing version constraints

Prefer version ranges for applications and libraries, such as fastapi>=0.115,<0.116. The lockfile records exact resolved versions for reproducible installs, so use exact pins in pyproject.toml only when a specific version is required.

docs.title: Add a Dependency from a Git Repository
docs.text:
uv can add a package directly from a Git repository:

uv add "flask @ git+https://github.com/pallets/flask"

Instead of putting the Git URL directly in [project].dependencies, uv adds the package name there and records the repository location under [tool.uv.sources]. After this command, the complete project file looks like this:

[project]
name = "license-service"
version = "0.1.0"
requires-python = ">=3.11"
dependencies = [
    "fastapi>=0.115,<0.116", # Allow patch releases in 0.115
    "flask",
    "httpx==0.27.2", # Require this exact version
    "requests>=2.32.3", # Set a minimum version
]

[tool.uv.sources]
flask = { git = "https://github.com/pallets/flask" }

docs.title: Dependency Groups
docs.text:
Development tools, test frameworks, and documentation generators are not needed in production. Dependency groups separate them from runtime requirements:

DevDocs

Add test and development tools to the dev group with --group. The dev group is special-cased, so --dev can also be used as a shortcut:

uv add --group dev pytest
uv add --dev ruff

Add MkDocs to a separate docs group:

uv add --group docs "mkdocs>=1.6.1,<2.0"

After these commands, the complete project file looks like this:

[project]
name = "license-service"
version = "0.1.0"
requires-python = ">=3.11"
dependencies = [
    "fastapi>=0.115,<0.116", # Allow patch releases in 0.115
    "flask",
    "httpx==0.27.2", # Require this exact version
    "requests>=2.32.3", # Set a minimum version
]

[dependency-groups]
dev = [
    "pytest>=8.0",
    "ruff>=0.15",
]
docs = [
    "mkdocs>=1.6.1,<2.0",
]

[tool.uv.sources]
flask = { git = "https://github.com/pallets/flask" }

docs.title: Dependency Markers
docs.text:
Some packages are available only on specific platforms or Python versions, so PEP 508 environment markers let you declare them only where they can be installed. For example, a Flask web app can use pywin32 for Windows Integrated Authentication; uv add accepts markers with --marker, so you can restrict pywin32 to Windows. See uv's common markers for other platform and Python-version conditions used in mixed environments such as Windows, Linux, WSL, CI, and production containers.

uv add "pywin32>=310" --marker "sys_platform == 'win32'"

After this command, the complete project file looks like this:

[project]
name = "license-service"
version = "0.1.0"
requires-python = ">=3.11"
dependencies = [
    "fastapi>=0.115,<0.116", # Allow patch releases in 0.115
    "flask",
    "httpx==0.27.2", # Require this exact version
    "pywin32>=310; sys_platform == 'win32'", # Windows-only
    "requests>=2.32.3", # Set a minimum version
]

[dependency-groups]
dev = [
    "pytest>=8.0",
    "ruff>=0.15",
]
docs = [
    "mkdocs>=1.6.1,<2.0",
]

[tool.uv.sources]
flask = { git = "https://github.com/pallets/flask" }

docs.title: Remove Dependencies
docs.text:
Use uv remove to remove a dependency. Choose the matching command for a normal or grouped dependency:

Normal DependenciesGrouped Dependencies

Remove a runtime dependency:

uv remove requests

Remove a dependency from the dev group:

uv remove --group dev pytest

If you run both commands, the complete project file looks like this:

[project]
name = "license-service"
version = "0.1.0"
requires-python = ">=3.11"
dependencies = [
    "fastapi>=0.115,<0.116", # Allow patch releases in 0.115
    "flask",
    "httpx==0.27.2", # Require this exact version
    "pywin32>=310; sys_platform == 'win32'", # Windows-only
]

[dependency-groups]
dev = [
    "ruff>=0.15",
]
docs = [
    "mkdocs>=1.6.1,<2.0",
]

[tool.uv.sources]
flask = { git = "https://github.com/pallets/flask" }

docs.title: The Lockfile
docs.text:
The uv.lock file is a TOML file generated by uv next to pyproject.toml. It records exact dependency versions, their relationships, package sources, and download hashes across the project's supported operating systems and Python versions. It is kept under version control and updated and reviewed alongside pyproject.toml so development, CI, and production can reuse the same reviewed versions.

The uv lock command resolves the requirements declared in pyproject.toml and creates or updates the lockfile without creating a project virtual environment or installing packages. It may download package metadata, wheels, or source archives during resolution. It preserves existing locked versions where possible and leaves an up-to-date lockfile unchanged, even when newer versions are available.

uv lock

The following code block is an excerpt of uv.lock, with download entries and other packages omitted for readability. Each [[package]] entry describes a resolved package: FastAPI is locked to 0.115.14, which satisfies the declared range, and Starlette is one of its transitive dependencies. A package's dependencies list identifies the packages it requires, whose resolved versions are recorded in their own [[package]] entries. Here, FastAPI requires Starlette, which in turn requires AnyIO. The top-level version and revision describe the lockfile format, not the project's version.

version = 1
revision = 3
requires-python = ">=3.11"

[[package]]
name = "fastapi"
version = "0.115.14"
source = { registry = "https://pypi.org/simple" }
dependencies = [
    { name = "pydantic" },
    { name = "starlette" },
    { name = "typing-extensions" },
]

[[package]]
name = "starlette"
version = "0.46.2"
source = { registry = "https://pypi.org/simple" }
dependencies = [
    { name = "anyio" },
]

Commands that update the lockfile

uv lock, uv add, uv remove, uv sync, uv run, uv tree, and uv export create or update uv.lock as needed.

docs.title: Upgrade the Lockfile
docs.text:
The uv lock --upgrade command resolves all dependencies to the latest versions allowed by the constraints in pyproject.toml. Use --upgrade-package instead to upgrade a specific dependency while retaining other locked versions where possible.

Single DependencyAll Dependencies

Upgrade a single dependency to the latest version its constraint allows, retaining other locked versions where possible.

uv lock --upgrade-package fastapi

Upgrade all dependencies to the latest versions allowed by their declared ranges.

uv lock --upgrade

Install the updated versions into the project's virtual environment:

uv sync

docs.title: Validate the Lockfile
docs.text:
The uv lock --check command validates that the lockfile is in sync with pyproject.toml without modifying it. Use it in CI or before committing to catch outdated lockfiles:

uv lock --check

docs.title: Default Synchronization
docs.text:
Local Development

Use the default sync for day-to-day development. It keeps the virtual environment aligned with the project metadata and, by default, installs the project in editable mode with the configured default dependency groups.

The uv sync command prepares a project's Python environment by installing the dependency versions recorded in uv.lock. It creates an in-project virtual environment (.venv) if needed and installs, upgrades, downgrades, or removes packages to match the selected dependencies and dependency groups. If the lockfile is outdated relative to pyproject.toml, it re-locks automatically before installing.

DefaultDependency GroupAll Groups

Install dependencies from project.dependencies in pyproject.toml and the default dependency groups, including their transitive dependencies (packages those dependencies require). The dev group is included by default unless tool.uv.default-groups changes that selection.

uv sync

Include a dependency group alongside project.dependencies and the default groups. This example explicitly selects dev, which is normally already included by default.

uv sync --group dev

Install project.dependencies and all dependency groups, but not optional extras unless explicitly requested.

uv sync --all-groups

docs.title: Frozen Installs
docs.text:
Intermediate Docker Layers

Use frozen syncs in intermediate Docker layers or workspace builds when dependencies need to be installed before all project source files are available. Because --frozen skips lockfile freshness checks, validate the lockfile separately and run a final --locked sync once all project files are present. See uv's intermediate-layer guidance.

The uv sync --frozen command performs frozen installs that use the dependency versions recorded in an existing lockfile without checking whether it matches the declarations in pyproject.toml or updating it. Any dependency change in pyproject.toml is therefore not resolved into a new lockfile during the sync.

uv sync --frozen [--no-install-project] [--no-install-workspace]
  • --no-install-project: Skips installing the project itself while still installing its dependencies.
  • --no-install-workspace: Installs only dependencies, not workspace projects.

docs.title: Locked Installs
docs.text:
CI/CD and Production Builds

Locked, non-editable installs suit production targets and CI/CD steps that prepare deployment artifacts. Typical locations are GitHub Actions workflow files and Dockerfile build steps. Kubernetes Manifests can also run the command through container command and args fields, though installing dependencies during the image build avoids startup-time downloads.

The uv sync --locked command performs locked installs that prepare the project environment using the dependency versions recorded in uv.lock, while checking that the lockfile matches the declarations in pyproject.toml. If the lockfile is missing or stale, the command fails rather than changing it automatically, requiring it to be created or updated and reviewed before the build proceeds. The pyproject.toml must define a [build-system] for uv sync to install the project itself. See uv's editable installation guidance.

EditableNon-Editable

By default, uv sync installs the project and workspace members in editable mode, so imports use their source checkout and reflect source edits without reinstalling.

uv sync --locked

With --no-editable, the project is installed into the virtual environment as a regular Python package, so Python imports the installed files rather than your source files directly. The installed package can still be imported if you move or remove the source folder, however, editing source files does not change the installed version.

For example, a package named sync_demo on Python 3.12 is installed under .venv/lib/python3.12/site-packages/sync_demo/, alongside sync_demo-0.1.0.dist-info/, which stores its name, version, and other package information. A regular sync may reuse that installation. To apply your edits, use the optional --reinstall-package sync-demo flag to force rebuilding and reinstalling. Running a source file directly still executes your edited code.

uv sync --locked --no-editable [--reinstall-package sync-demo]

docs.title: Resolution Strategies
docs.text:
Before writing a lockfile, uv resolves direct and transitive dependencies to find versions that satisfy all declared constraints. It does this automatically when dependencies are added, updated, or synchronized and, by default, selects the latest compatible version of each dependency.

For libraries, testing only against the latest versions is insufficient: a declaration such as fastapi>=0.100.0 claims compatibility with every version from 0.100.0 upward, not just the newest release.

All DependenciesDirect Dependencies

Install the lowest compatible versions for all direct and transitive dependencies:

uv sync --resolution lowest

Install the lowest compatible versions for direct dependencies only, keeping transitive dependencies at their latest:

uv sync --resolution lowest-direct

docs.title: Inspect the Graph
docs.text:
Display the resolved dependency tree, showing which package pulled in which transitive dependency:

uv tree

docs.title: Share a Requirements File
docs.text:
When another tool expects a requirements.txt, export one from the project's lockfile:

uv export --format requirements.txt -o requirements.txt

Keep pyproject.toml and uv.lock as the project's source of truth; regenerate the export after changing dependencies. For working directly with an existing requirements.txt, see Standalone Environments and Tools.

docs.title: Standalone Environments and Tools with uv
Introduction
docs.text: Not every task needs a pyproject.toml project. uv can also work with an existing requirements.txt, run a single script, or provide a command-line tool. For the project-managed workflow, start with Project Scaffolding with uv.

docs.title: Create a Standalone Environment
docs.text:
In a directory containing a requirements.txt, create a virtual environment manually:

uv venv

This creates .venv in the current directory. To choose an interpreter explicitly, use this form instead:

uv venv --python 3.12

In a managed project, uv sync creates and maintains .venv for you; uv venv is most useful when you are managing an environment yourself.

docs.title: Install from requirements.txt
docs.text:
Install the existing requirements into .venv:

uv pip install -r requirements.txt

To inspect what was installed, list the packages:

uv pip list

uv pip works directly on the environment: it does not update pyproject.toml or uv.lock. For a managed project, use uv add instead.

docs.title: Run a Script with uv run
docs.text:
Run a small script without creating a project:

uv run --no-project report.py

--no-project keeps the script independent even if you happen to run it inside a project directory.

docs.title: Declare Inline Dependencies
docs.text:
Initialize a script with metadata for its Python version and dependencies:

uv init --script report.py --python 3.12

Add a package needed by that script:

uv add --script report.py rich

uv writes the requirement into a small metadata block at the top of the file, so the script carries its own setup instructions. Run it without managing a .venv yourself:

uv run report.py

docs.title: Run a Tool Once with uvx
docs.text:
Try Ruff without adding it to the project:

uvx ruff check .

uvx is shorthand for uv tool run; the equivalent command is:

uv tool run ruff check .

Both use an isolated tool environment. If a tool needs your project's dependencies, add it to the project and use uv run instead.

docs.title: Install and Maintain Tools with uv tool
docs.text:
Install a frequently used tool for your user account:

uv tool install ruff

See which tools are installed:

uv tool list

Upgrade a tool when needed:

uv tool upgrade ruff

Remove it when you no longer need it:

uv tool uninstall ruff

docs.title: Choose the Right Workflow
docs.text:
Need Start with Develop a pyproject.toml project uv sync, uv add, uv run Use an existing requirements.txt uv venv, uv pip install -r requirements.txt Run a self-contained script uv run --no-project or inline script dependencies Try a CLI tool once uvx Keep a CLI tool available uv tool install

If another workflow needs a requirements.txt from a managed project, see Export Dependencies.

docs.title: Dependency Caching with uv
docs.text: uv caches package metadata, downloaded wheels, and wheels built from source. A project environment (.venv) is normally beside pyproject.toml; it is not the package cache. The Bob Follows the Cache notebook runs the same experiments as this section. Run the commands below from /workspace in the lab's Dev Container, in order. A first run needs network access.

docs.title: Applied Lab
docs.text: The lab locks NumPy, SciPy, and Matplotlib and builds a local uv-cache-demo wheel containing a generated 16 MiB synthetic matrix. Its fixture is deterministic and not a trained model. Downloaded numerical-library wheels make cache growth visible; the locally built wheel makes CI pruning visible. The container supplies uv 0.13.3 (for the centralized-environment preview), Python 3.12, and Jupyter, but does not install the project or populate its uv cache at startup. The separate CI workflow pins uv 0.11.1. The lab's UV_LINK_MODE=copy keeps installed files independent of the cache. The container's cache is separate from your host's.

docs.title: Environment Variables That Influence Cache Behavior
docs.text:
These variables configure where uv caches data, whether it can reuse it, and how it installs files from the cache. See the uv environment variable reference for the complete list.

Variable Cache behavior UV_CACHE_DIR Selects the shared cache directory instead of the system default; equivalent to --cache-dir. UV_NO_CACHE Uses a temporary cache for that invocation rather than the persistent cache; equivalent to --no-cache. UV_OFFLINE Disables network access, requiring cached or local packages; equivalent to --offline. UV_LINK_MODE Chooses clone (copy-on-write when supported), hardlink (shared files on one filesystem), copy (independent files), or symlink (depends on the cache). Defaults to clone on Linux/macOS and hardlink on Windows. UV_LOCK_TIMEOUT Sets how long uv waits for a cache lock, including when other uv processes are using the cache. UV_CONCURRENT_CACHE_READS Controls threads reading cached HTTP responses; defaults to 4.

docs.title: Commands That Populate the Cache
docs.text:
Package operations populate or reuse cache entries; cleanup commands remove them. For project locking and syncing, see Dependency Management with uv.

Command Effect on the cache uv pip install {pkg} Reuses or adds package metadata and wheels. --refresh revalidates cached data; --refresh-package {pkg} limits that to one package. uv add {pkg} Adds a dependency, resolves and synchronizes the project, and reuses or adds cached packages. uv sync Synchronizes a project from its lockfile, using or adding cached packages. uv tool install {tool} Installs a tool in its own environment while sharing uv's package cache. uv cache prune Removes unused entries and centralized project environments. With --ci, also removes prebuilt wheels and unzipped source distributions while retaining source-built wheels. uv cache clean [package] Removes all cache entries, or entries for only the named package.

docs.title: Build Configuration and Wheel Reuse
docs.text:
For a local package, tool.uv.cache-keys in pyproject.toml defines which build inputs invalidate a cached wheel. Keys replace uv's default checks: include every input that affects the build. A key containing only pyproject.toml, for example, may miss source-only changes. These configurations illustrate three ways to track inputs:

FilesGit CommitEnvironment Variable

Track the manifest and an additional dependency file used by the build.

[tool.uv]
cache-keys = [{ file = "pyproject.toml" }, { file = "requirements.txt" }]

Track the manifest and Git commit when the build depends on version control; add tags = true if tags affect it too. A commit key alone will not detect uncommitted source edits.

[tool.uv]
cache-keys = [{ file = "pyproject.toml" }, { git = { commit = true } }]

Track the manifest and a build-setting variable, whose changed value forces a rebuild.

[tool.uv]
cache-keys = [{ file = "pyproject.toml" }, { env = "MY_BUILD_SETTING" }]

The lab's content fingerprint

This lab uses cache-keys = [{ env = "CACHE_DEMO_KEY" }]. After generating the fixture, scripts/build_key.py hashes pyproject.toml, Python source, JSON, and bundled data. Supply its result to every sync that installs the local package. Identical content can reuse a wheel across fresh CI checkouts even when file timestamps differ. --no-editable installs that wheel instead of linking the source tree.

docs.title: Populate and Inspect the Cache
docs.text:
uv organizes cached data into distinct target types. These include Prebuilt Wheels downloaded from package indexes, Source-built Wheels built locally, and Unpacked Source Distributions used during builds. When enabled, Centralized Project Environments are also cached so a project can reuse its installed packages.

Downloaded wheelsLocally built wheelUnzipped source distributionCentralized project environmentOther Unused Cache Entries

Prebuilt Wheels are downloaded from package indexes and can be installed without building the package from source. uv caches them so later installs can reuse them instead of downloading them again.

Create an ignored directory for the disposable experiments in later tabs.

mkdir -p lab

Create the project environment for the following experiments.

uv venv --python 3.12

Install a small numerical-computing stack directly with uv pip install. --only-binary :all: selects prebuilt wheels when available.

uv pip install \
  --python .venv/bin/python \
  --only-binary :all: \
  numpy \
  scipy \
  matplotlib

Measure the populated cache; cache-size is a preview feature in this uv version.

uv cache size --human --preview-features cache-size

Source-built Wheels are built locally from source packages and stored in the cache. Reusing a cached wheel avoids repeating the build when its inputs have not changed.

Generate the deterministic 16 MiB fixture before building the local package.

.venv/bin/python scripts/generate_fixture.py

Install the project as a regular wheel; the content fingerprint determines when uv rebuilds it.

CACHE_DEMO_KEY=$(.venv/bin/python scripts/build_key.py) \
uv sync \
  --locked \
  --no-editable \
  --python 3.12

Run the installed package and write a PNG report.

.venv/bin/python -m uv_cache_demo.main --output reports/embeddings.png

Locate the locally built wheel; its path is the checkpoint for later pruning.

find "$(uv cache dir)" -type f -name 'uv_cache_demo-*.whl' -print

Unpacked Source Distributions are extracted source trees that uv uses to build wheels. uv can cache both the unpacked source and the wheel produced from it.

Force a source build of small idna into an ignored target, without changing the project's lockfile.

uv pip install \
  --python "$(uv python find 3.12)" \
  --target lab/sdist-target \
  --no-deps \
  --no-binary idna \
  'idna==3.10'

Inspect source-cache buckets; their version suffixes are internal details and may change.

find "$(uv cache dir)" -type d -name 'sdists-v*' -print

Locate uv's unpacked idna source (src/idna) while it is still present.

find "$(uv cache dir)" -type d -path '*/sdists-v*/pypi/idna/3.10/*/src/idna' -print

Find the idna wheel built from that source, distinct from the downloaded numerical-library wheels.

find "$(uv cache dir)" -type f -name 'idna-*.whl' -print

Centralized Project Environments store a project's installed packages in uv's cache instead of beside pyproject.toml. The opt-in centralized-project-envs preview feature connects .venv to the cached environment, usually with a link.

Create an ignored, disposable project to keep the main .venv separate.

mkdir -p lab/centralized

Copy the locked project declarations into that directory; the project itself will not be installed there.

cp pyproject.toml uv.lock lab/centralized/

Populate the cached environment without specifying UV_PROJECT_ENVIRONMENT or --active: explicit environment paths bypass centralization.

uv --preview-features centralized-project-envs sync \
  --directory lab/centralized \
  --locked \
  --no-install-project \
  --python 3.12

Inspect the .venv link pointing into uv's cache (uv may use a path file if linking is unavailable).

ls -ld lab/centralized/.venv

Check that dependencies import from the new environment rather than the main project's .venv.

lab/centralized/.venv/bin/python -c 'import numpy; print(numpy.__version__)'

Other Unused Cache Entries are classified by cache metadata and references, not installation status. An older uv may create cache entries in a format a newer version does not recognize; those entries can be removed while the installed package remains in .venv or --target. Unreferenced unpacked wheel archives may also be considered unused, but a current-format wheel is not unused just because its package is uninstalled.

Create a directory for the disposable package installs.

mkdir -p lab/prune-probe

Use uv 0.4.12 through uvx to install a prebuilt packaging wheel into an ignored target.

UV_CACHE_DIR="$HOME/.cache/uvx-prune-bootstrap" \
  uvx --from 'uv==0.4.12' uv \
  --cache-dir "$(uv cache dir)" \
  pip install \
  --python "$(uv python find 3.12)" \
  --target lab/prune-probe/old-wheel \
  --reinstall \
  --no-deps \
  --only-binary packaging \
  'packaging==24.2'

Use the same old uv version to build a wheel from the idna source distribution.

UV_CACHE_DIR="$HOME/.cache/uvx-prune-bootstrap" \
  uvx --from 'uv==0.4.12' uv \
  --cache-dir "$(uv cache dir)" \
  pip install \
  --python "$(uv python find 3.12)" \
  --target lab/prune-probe/old-sdist \
  --reinstall \
  --no-deps \
  --no-binary idna \
  'idna==3.10'

Inspect the cache buckets created by both the current and older uv versions; bucket names and versions are implementation details and may change.

find "$(uv cache dir)" -mindepth 1 -maxdepth 1 -type d -printf '%f\n' | sort

docs.title: Offline Synchronization
docs.text:
Remove just the installed environment, leaving uv's cache available.

rm -rf .venv

Restore it without network access; the fixture and build fingerprint are still available.

CACHE_DEMO_KEY=$("$(uv python find 3.12)" scripts/build_key.py) \
  uv sync \
  --locked \
  --no-editable \
  --offline \
  --python 3.12

Confirm that NumPy and the local wheel import from .venv.

.venv/bin/python -c 'import numpy, uv_cache_demo; print(numpy.__file__, uv_cache_demo.__file__)'

docs.title: Compare UV_LINK_MODE
docs.text:
Use four disposable environments to compare installation modes without changing the main .venv. Each tab synchronizes the locked dependencies into a separate environment; --offline ensures these trials reuse the cached wheels. On a bind-mounted workspace, hardlink or clone may fall back to copying if the cache and environment are on different filesystems.

CloneCopyHardlinkSymlink

Sync into a disposable environment with clone, uv's normal Linux/macOS mode. Where supported, the environment initially shares disk blocks with the cache, then gets separate blocks when files change. This can use less disk space than making full copies.

UV_PROJECT_ENVIRONMENT=lab/clone \
  UV_LINK_MODE=clone \
  uv sync \
  --locked \
  --no-install-project \
  --offline \
  --python 3.12

Inspect the installed file and its hard-link count; stat alone cannot prove whether copy-on-write cloning occurred.

stat -c '%F; hard links: %h' lab/clone/lib/python3.12/site-packages/numpy/__init__.py

Verify the installed NumPy version.

lab/clone/bin/python -c 'import numpy; print(numpy.__version__)'

Sync using copy to make independent files in the environment. This uses more disk space than shared-block modes, but changes to installed files do not change the cached files.

UV_PROJECT_ENVIRONMENT=lab/copy \
  UV_LINK_MODE=copy \
  uv sync \
  --locked \
  --no-install-project \
  --offline \
  --python 3.12

Inspect the installed file's type and link count.

stat -c '%F; hard links: %h' lab/copy/lib/python3.12/site-packages/numpy/__init__.py

Use hardlink to let the environment and cache share the same file on one filesystem, which saves disk space. Editing a hardlinked file also changes the cached file. If they are on different filesystems, uv falls back to making a copy.

UV_PROJECT_ENVIRONMENT=lab/hardlink \
  UV_LINK_MODE=hardlink \
  uv sync \
  --locked \
  --no-install-project \
  --offline \
  --python 3.12

Check whether the installed file has multiple hard links (%h greater than one).

stat -c '%F; hard links: %h' lab/hardlink/lib/python3.12/site-packages/numpy/__init__.py

Use symlink to make the environment's files point to files in the cache, avoiding separate copies. The environment depends on those cache paths, so cleaning or moving the cache can break it.

UV_PROJECT_ENVIRONMENT=lab/symlink \
  UV_LINK_MODE=symlink \
  uv sync \
  --locked \
  --no-install-project \
  --offline \
  --python 3.12

Inspect a link target to see why cleaning the cache would break this installation.

readlink lab/symlink/lib/python3.12/site-packages/numpy/__init__.py

Remove this disposable environment before the cleanup stages; retain the copy-mode .venv.

rm -rf lab/symlink

docs.title: Cache Cleanup Operations
docs.text:
uv provides different Cleanup Operations, each with its own rules for deciding what to remove from the cache. Depending on the command, cleanup may affect Prebuilt Wheels, Source-built Wheels, Unpacked Source Distributions, and Centralized Project Environments, as well as other Unused Cache Entries. The disk space reclaimed by each operation depends on the cache contents and artifact sizes, so a broader cleanup does not necessarily reclaim more space in a particular run.

Normal pruneCI pruneComplete Clean

The uv cache prune command performs the standard cleanup by removing Unused Cache Entries and all Centralized Project Environments. Unused entries may include Prebuilt Wheels, Unpacked Source Distributions, and Source-built Wheels. It retains entries that uv still considers in use, unlike uv cache clean, which removes every cache entry. Run the ordinary prune command:

uv cache prune

Confirm that the obsolete cache buckets created by uv 0.4.12 are gone. They contained the old packaging wheel and old idna built wheel.

find "$(uv cache dir)" -maxdepth 1 -type d \
  \( -name 'wheels-v1' -o -name 'built-wheels-v3' \) \
  -print

Confirm that the current prebuilt wheel entries for NumPy, SciPy, and Matplotlib remain.

find "$(uv cache dir)" -type d \
  \( -path '*/wheels-v*/pypi/numpy' \
    -o -path '*/wheels-v*/pypi/scipy' \
    -o -path '*/wheels-v*/pypi/matplotlib' \) \
  -print

Confirm that the current-format wheels built from the local project and idna source remain.

find "$(uv cache dir)" -type f \
  \( -name 'uv_cache_demo-*.whl' -o -name 'idna-*.whl' \) \
  -print

Confirm that the unpacked idna source remains after ordinary pruning.

find "$(uv cache dir)" -type d \
  -path '*/sdists-v*/pypi/idna/3.10/*/src/idna' \
  -print

Confirm that pruning has not removed the packages installed into --target.

test -d lab/prune-probe/old-wheel/packaging
test -d lab/prune-probe/old-sdist/idna

Confirm the main, non-centralized .venv remains usable.

.venv/bin/python -c 'import numpy; print(numpy.__version__)'

Measure the cache size after pruning.

uv cache size --human --preview-features cache-size

The uv cache prune --ci command is designed for CI environments. To support this strategy, it retains current-format Source-built Wheels, which can take significant time and computing resources to build and can save time in later CI runs. It removes Prebuilt Wheels and Unpacked Source Distributions to reduce cache size as those are generally quick to download again. The command also performs ordinary pruning, so it can remove obsolete source-built wheels. Run the CI-specific prune command:

uv cache prune --ci

Confirm that the obsolete cache buckets created by uv 0.4.12 are gone. They contained the old packaging wheel and old idna built wheel.

find "$(uv cache dir)" -maxdepth 1 -type d \
  \( -name 'wheels-v1' -o -name 'built-wheels-v3' \) \
  -print

Confirm that the prebuilt wheel entries for NumPy, SciPy, and Matplotlib are gone (no output expected).

find "$(uv cache dir)" -type d \
  \( -path '*/wheels-v*/pypi/numpy' \
    -o -path '*/wheels-v*/pypi/scipy' \
    -o -path '*/wheels-v*/pypi/matplotlib' \) \
  -print

Confirm that the current-format wheels built from the local project and idna source remain.

find "$(uv cache dir)" -type f \
  \( -name 'uv_cache_demo-*.whl' -o -name 'idna-*.whl' \) \
  -print

Check that the unzipped idna source is gone (no output expected).

find "$(uv cache dir)" -type d -path '*/sdists-v*/pypi/idna/3.10/*/src/idna' -print

Verify the saved centralized environment target is gone; its .venv link may be dangling.

test ! -d "$(cat lab/centralized-target)"

Confirm that pruning has not removed the packages installed into --target.

test -d lab/prune-probe/old-wheel/packaging
test -d lab/prune-probe/old-sdist/idna

Measure the cache size after pruning.

uv cache size --human --preview-features cache-size

Confirm that installed packages in the main copy-mode .venv still import.

.venv/bin/python -c 'import numpy; from uv_cache_demo.main import cache_message; print(cache_message())'

The uv cache clean command removes All Cache Entries, including Prebuilt Wheels, Unpacked Source Distributions, Source-built Wheels, and Centralized Project Environments. Since every cache target is in scope, this is the most aggressive cleanup command. Run the complete cleanup:

uv cache clean

Confirm that the old cache buckets are gone (no output expected).

find "$(uv cache dir)" -maxdepth 1 -type d \
  \( -name 'wheels-v1' -o -name 'built-wheels-v3' \) \
  -print

Confirm that the NumPy, SciPy, and Matplotlib prebuilt wheel entries are gone (no output expected).

find "$(uv cache dir)" -type d \
  \( -path '*/wheels-v*/pypi/numpy' \
    -o -path '*/wheels-v*/pypi/scipy' \
    -o -path '*/wheels-v*/pypi/matplotlib' \) \
  -print

Measure the emptied cache; uv may retain housekeeping files.

uv cache size --human --preview-features cache-size

Verify that the local and idna source-built wheels are no longer cached (no output expected).

find "$(uv cache dir)" -type f \
  \( -name 'uv_cache_demo-*.whl' -o -name 'idna-*.whl' \) \
  -print

Verify that the unpacked idna source is no longer cached (no output expected).

find "$(uv cache dir)" -type d \
  -path '*/sdists-v*/pypi/idna/3.10/*/src/idna' \
  -print

Verify that the centralized environment target is gone (no output expected).

test ! -d "$(cat lab/centralized-target)"

Confirm that cleanup has not removed the packages installed into --target.

test -d lab/prune-probe/old-wheel/packaging
test -d lab/prune-probe/old-sdist/idna

Confirm installed copies still work. A symlink-mode environment would instead depend on the removed cache paths.

.venv/bin/python -c 'import numpy; from uv_cache_demo.main import cache_message; print(cache_message())'

Check that the previously generated report also remains in the workspace.

test -f reports/embeddings.png

The table compares five deliberately populated cache targets after each operation runs with uv 0.13.3. A check mark means the target was removed; a dash means it was retained. The obsolete-format entries were created with uv 0.4.12. Ordinary pruning can also remove orphaned current-format archives that are no longer referenced by current wheel or source buckets. uv cache clean removes other cache entries, such as metadata and index responses; in this probe, the cache root and lock file remain.

Target uv cache prune uv cache prune --ci uv cache clean Current-format prebuilt/downloaded wheel (wheels-v7) — ✓ ✓ Current-format source-built wheel (sdists-v10, .whl) — — ✓ Unpacked source distribution (sdists-v10, src/) — ✓ ✓ Centralized project environment (environments-v2) ✓ ✓ ✓ Obsolete-format entries from uv 0.4.12 (wheels-v1, built-wheels-v3, including its built wheel and sdist) ✓ ✓ ✓

docs.title: Using uv's Cache in CI Environments
docs.text: In CI workflows such as GitHub Actions, reusing uv's package cache avoids repeated downloads and builds. This page uses the repository's .github/workflows/uv-cache.yml workflow to compare cache strategies and measure their effects. Keeping large downloaded packages can save network traffic but increases the size and transfer time of the saved cache, so compare both strategies rather than assuming that the smaller cache is always faster.

docs.title: Used Project
docs.text:
This table lists the workflow and project files used in the examples.

Component Description .github/workflows/uv-cache.yml GitHub Actions workflow that compares full and CI-pruned caches and records install time and local cache size. notebooks/uv_cache_lab/pyproject.toml and uv.lock Define the package build configuration and locked dependencies installed by the workflow.

docs.title: CI Caching Pattern
docs.text:
The diagram below starts at Cache storage to show two ways of keeping package data between CI jobs:

  • Persistent runner: Reuse a cache directory outside the job's temporary workspace so cleanup does not delete it.
  • Temporary runner: Restore a saved cache using a key based on the platform and dependency files; if no matching cache is available, uv populates a new one during installation. The GitHub Actions example uses this approach.

Both paths recreate a fresh environment from the committed uv.lock. --locked fails if the lockfile needs updating; missing packages are downloaded or built and cached by uv. After the build, keep the full cache or prune it for CI, then save the cache (or retain its persistent directory) for the next job. Preserve the package cache rather than .venv, and include cache transfer time when comparing build durations.

flowchart TD
    start["Start CI build"] --> storage{"Cache storage"}
    storage -->|"Persistent Runner or Volume"| persistent["Reuse the persistent cache directory"]
    storage -->|"Temporary Runner"| key["Cache (Hash-)Key"]
    key --> restore["Restore saved cache or start empty"]
    persistent --> sync["Create a Fresh Environment from Locked Dependencies"]
    restore --> sync
    sync --> verify["Build package, run tests, ..."]
    verify --> prune["Keep the cache or retain only locally built packages"]
    prune --> retain["Save cache if needed or retain persistent directory"]
    retain -. "Next build" .-> start

docs.title: GitHub Actions Example
docs.text:
Compare the Cache Strategies

The uv cache workflow compares a full cache with a CI-pruned cache. For each variant, run once cold and once warm without changing dependencies or sources:

  • Warm cache: Set clean_cache: false to reuse restored packages. Set prune_cache: false to keep the full cache, or true to prune downloaded wheels after installation; the workflow uses separate cache-key suffixes for these strategies.
  • Cold cache: Set clean_cache: true to clear the restored cache before syncing. Keep the same prune_cache choice as the warm run.

The workflow uses fresh GitHub-hosted runners, recreates .venv from uv.lock, and reports installation time and cache size. GitHub's cache-sharing rules affect which saved caches a job can restore: pull requests can restore the target branch's cache but save only for that pull request. Entries expire after seven days without access, or earlier under storage pressure. Without an accessible matching cache, uv downloads or builds dependencies normally.

docs.title: Workflow Triggers
docs.text:
The workflow runs on pushes to main that change notebooks/uv_cache_lab/ or the workflow itself, and can be started manually. Manual runs expose independent prune_cache and clean_cache choices:

on:
  push:
    branches:
      - main
    paths:
      - "notebooks/uv_cache_lab/**"
      - ".github/workflows/uv-cache.yml"
  workflow_dispatch:
    inputs:
      prune_cache:
        description: "Run uv cache prune --ci after installation"
        type: boolean
        default: true
      clean_cache:
        description: "Run uv cache clean before installing (cold run)"
        type: boolean
        default: false

docs.title: Set the Cache Directory and Measure Its Initial Size
docs.text:
Initially, the workflow sets UV_CACHE_DIR under the runner's temporary storage and writes it to GITHUB_ENV so subsequent steps use the same path. The measurement does not create the cache; a fresh runner normally starts at 0 KiB.

- name: Measure cache at the beginning of the job
  id: cache_start
  env:
    UV_CACHE_DIR: ${{ runner.temp }}/uv-cache
  run: |
    echo "UV_CACHE_DIR=$UV_CACHE_DIR" >> "$GITHUB_ENV"
    kib=0
    if [[ -d "$UV_CACHE_DIR" ]]; then
      kib=$(du -sk "$UV_CACHE_DIR" | cut -f1)
    fi
    echo "Before restoration: ${kib} KiB"
    echo "kib=$kib" >> "$GITHUB_OUTPUT"

docs.title: Prepare the Fixture and Cache Key
docs.text:
Before restoring the cache, the workflow generates the synthetic fixture and fingerprints all build inputs. It writes CACHE_DEMO_KEY to $GITHUB_ENV for later steps. The project's pyproject.toml uses that fingerprint in tool.uv.cache-keys: unchanged content can reuse the local wheel after a fresh checkout, while changed content triggers a rebuild. This uv wheel-cache key differs from the GitHub Actions cache key described next.

- name: Generate fixture and fingerprint build inputs
  run: |
    python notebooks/uv_cache_lab/scripts/generate_fixture.py
    build_key=$(python notebooks/uv_cache_lab/scripts/build_key.py)
    echo "CACHE_DEMO_KEY=$build_key" >> "$GITHUB_ENV"

docs.title: Configure the Cache Key and Restore the Cache
docs.text:
astral-sh/setup-uv installs the pinned CI uv version (0.11.1) and restores or saves the shared cache when eligible. Unlike tool.uv.cache-keys, its GitHub cache key depends on inputs such as platform, cache-dependency-glob, and cache-suffix. The globs include the package's build inputs, so changed sources affect both keys.

- name: Set up uv and restore its package cache
  id: uv
  uses: astral-sh/setup-uv@v5
  with:
    version: "0.11.1"
    enable-cache: true
    cache-local-path: ${{ env.UV_CACHE_DIR }}
    cache-dependency-glob: |
      notebooks/uv_cache_lab/pyproject.toml
      notebooks/uv_cache_lab/uv.lock
      notebooks/uv_cache_lab/src/**/*.py
      notebooks/uv_cache_lab/src/**/*.json
      notebooks/uv_cache_lab/src/**/*.bin
    cache-suffix: ${{ env.PRUNE_CACHE == 'true' && 'embeddings-demo-ci-pruned' || 'embeddings-demo-full' }}
    prune-cache: false
  • enable-cache: Restores and saves uv's package cache across eligible runs.
  • cache-local-path: Matches the UV_CACHE_DIR used by uv and the measurements.
  • cache-dependency-glob: Hashes the manifest, lockfile, source, and generated fixture for the saved-cache key.
  • cache-suffix: Separates full (embeddings-demo-full) and CI-pruned (embeddings-demo-ci-pruned) caches.
  • prune-cache: Disables automatic pruning so the workflow can explicitly prune and measure the result, including on cache hits.

GitHub cannot overwrite an existing cache with the same key, even if a job prunes its local restored copy. The workflow records sizes in KiB for the local cache directory, not the compressed GitHub archive or .venv; optional steps are measured even when skipped.

docs.title: Clear the uv Cache for a Cold Install
docs.text:
With CLEAN_CACHE=true, the workflow clears the restored cache to simulate a cold install; otherwise it reuses cached packages. Either way it records the size afterward.

- name: Clear uv cache for a cold install
  id: cache_cleaned
  run: |
    if [[ "$CLEAN_CACHE" == "true" ]]; then
      uv cache clean
    fi
    kib=0
    if [[ -d "$UV_CACHE_DIR" ]]; then
      kib=$(du -sk "$UV_CACHE_DIR" | cut -f1)
    fi
    echo "After optional cleaning: ${kib} KiB"
    echo "kib=$kib" >> "$GITHUB_OUTPUT"

docs.title: Create a Fresh Environment from Locked Dependencies
docs.text:
The sync step recreates .venv from the committed lockfile and builds or reuses the local wheel. It times only uv sync; the size measurement happens after the timer.

- name: Create a fresh environment from locked dependencies
  id: install
  shell: bash
  run: |
    start_ms=$(date +%s%3N)
    uv sync --directory notebooks/uv_cache_lab --locked --no-editable --python 3.12
    end_ms=$(date +%s%3N)
    echo "milliseconds=$((end_ms - start_ms))" >> "$GITHUB_OUTPUT"
    kib=0
    if [[ -d "$UV_CACHE_DIR" ]]; then
      kib=$(du -sk "$UV_CACHE_DIR" | cut -f1)
    fi
    echo "After uv sync: ${kib} KiB"
    echo "kib=$kib" >> "$GITHUB_OUTPUT"

docs.title: Generate the Embedding Report
docs.text:
After syncing, the workflow analyzes the installed synthetic embeddings and saves its report under the runner's temporary directory.

- name: Analyze the installed embeddings and generate a report
  run: |
    notebooks/uv_cache_lab/.venv/bin/python -m uv_cache_demo.main \
      --output "${{ runner.temp }}/embeddings.png"

docs.title: Keep the Cache or Retain Only Locally Built Packages
docs.text:
After the report, PRUNE_CACHE controls whether uv cache prune --ci discards dependency downloads while retaining built wheels. Future jobs may need to download the numerical libraries again. The 16 MiB bundled fixture makes the retained local wheel visible; wheel size does not imply an expensive rebuild or a guaranteed speedup. The workflow records the final cache size even when pruning is skipped.

- name: Keep the cache or retain locally built packages
  id: cache_size
  shell: bash
  run: |
    if [[ "$PRUNE_CACHE" == "true" ]]; then
      uv cache prune --ci
    fi
    kib=0
